clue.text: It's beside the point

parts.note: reads like a dismissal of something irrelevant, but literally describes a figure written next to the dot in a number such as 3.14

explanation.surface: Someone brushes off a remark as irrelevant.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'beside the point' means irrelevant; taken literally it places the thing next to the decimal point.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraction written in tenths and hundredths sits immediately to the right of the dot separating whole units.

clue.text: A fellow who adds up the accounts of course

parts.note: a don is a university fellow
to cast accounts is an old phrase for adding them up, so one who does it is a caster

explanation.surface: A college fellow who balances the books, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally', but it means 'belonging to a racecourse': Doncaster is the town whose course stages the St Leger.
explanation.definitionFit: This Yorkshire town is famous for its racecourse, home of the St Leger horse race.

clue.text: Favoured by the flourishing composer

parts.note: 'flourishing' suggests a successful composer, but literally means one fond of ornamental flourishes in music

explanation.surface: A successful composer's favourite device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flourishing' looks like 'prospering' but means writing showy passages: the answer is the elaborate solo passage near the end of a concerto movement.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an ornamental solo passage, often improvised, letting a performer display virtuosity.

clue.text: Develop green arms, and you'll get the bird

indicators.note: to develop something is to work it into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fanciful instruction: grow green limbs and you will turn into a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Develop' signals the anagram of GREEN ARMS.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a fish-eating diving duck with a saw-edged bill.

clue.text: Bird singing to St. Peter ?

parts.note: Shakespeare's 'Hark, hark, the ... at heaven's gate sings', and St Peter keeps heaven's gate

explanation.surface: A bird serenading the keeper of heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: The song in Cymbeline has this bird singing 'at heaven's gate', where St Peter traditionally keeps the keys.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's songbird sings at heaven's gate, the post St Peter guards.

clue.text: Science taken in doses

definitions.meaning: a branch of natural science dealing with matter and energy
'physic' is an old word for medicine, and ... are medicines swallowed in measured amounts

explanation.surface: A subject absorbed a little at a time, like a student cramming.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense uses the archaic 'physic' for a medicine, as in 'take physic, pomp'.
explanation.definitionFit: It names both the study of matter and motion and, archaically, remedies a doctor prescribes.

clue.text: Stout plans to provide candidates

indicators.note: the plans are worked over to provide something new, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Ambitious schemes are drawn up to supply applicants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To provide' is the anagram signal on STOUT PLANS.
explanation.definitionFit: These are people seeking admission to a religious order, on probation before acceptance.

clue.text: You lose your duck, and ten score one-it's a plant!

indicators.note: to lose something is to be without it, so a letter is taken out of the word you

parts.note: taken as the word you
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, the figure 0, written as O
ten twenties make two hundred, CC in Roman numerals
A means one

explanation.surface: A batsman is out for nothing, the team scores two hundred and one, and a plant appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose' removes O, a duck (a cricketer's score of nought), from YOU, leaving YU. Ten score is 200, CC in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a spiky-leaved American shrub often grown as a houseplant.

clue.text: Inversely the long and the short of it?

definitions.text: Inversely the long and the short of it?

parts.words: Inversely the long and the short of it?
parts.note: 'the long and the short of it' means the gist, but read literally and reversed it is short-then-long syllables

explanation.surface: Someone sums up a matter, backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The metrical foot here is a short syllable followed by a long one, the reverse of 'long and short'.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse built of feet each made of an unstressed syllable then a stressed one is so named.

clue.text: A Dickensian nipper

parts.note: 'nipper' looks like a child, but Nipper is the surname of a maid in Dombey and Son

explanation.surface: A street urchin from a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nipper' suggests a small child; in Dombey and Son, Florence's sharp-tongued maid is Miss Nipper, whose first name is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens gave Florence Dombey's maid this first name and the surname Nipper.

clue.text: One can't sink lower than this

definitions.text: One can't sink lower than this

parts.words: One can't sink lower than this
parts.note: sounds like a moral judgment on bad behaviour, but describes the lowest point of anything, as of a career or of the sky beneath an observer

explanation.surface: An exasperated verdict on someone's disgraceful conduct.
explanation.definitionFit: In astronomy it is the point directly below the observer, and figuratively the lowest ebb of fortune.

clue.text: Where people are intent on leisure?

definitions.text: Where people are intent on leisure?

parts.words: Where people are intent on leisure?
parts.note: 'intent' reads as 'keen', but split it as 'in tent': holidaymakers sleeping under canvas while they relax

explanation.surface: A place where everyone is determined to relax.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'intent' as 'in tent': the people are under canvas, which places them at a holiday or military rest site.
explanation.definitionFit: Such sites are encampments set up for soldiers or travellers to recuperate, usually under canvas.

clue.text: A book for the gardener

parts.note: hints at a yearly gift book, but a gardener's version is a plant that lives a single season

explanation.surface: A present chosen for someone who loves gardening.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a yearly book (children's Christmas books in Britain) and a plant completing its life in one year.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a yearbook published every twelve months and a flower that grows, seeds and dies within one season.

clue.text: Outcome of sweated labour

parts.note: 'sweated labour' suggests exploited workers, but read literally the result of toiling is perspiration

explanation.surface: A complaint about the products of sweatshop exploitation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweated labour' means underpaid factory work; literally, hard work produces sweating, which is what the Latin-derived word means.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a formal term for perspiring, the body producing moisture through the skin.

clue.text: A pair of kings and a joker? Nonsense !

parts.note: Edward is the name of several English kings
Lear is Shakespeare's legendary British king

explanation.surface: A card hand of two kings and a joker, dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The hand of cards is a red herring: the two kings are a name borne by English monarchs and Shakespeare's Lear, together making the Victorian writer of nonsense verse.
explanation.definitionFit: This Victorian humorist wrote limericks and nonsense poems such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat.

clue.text: It may be easier to get into, than out of, these vehicles

definitions.text: It may be easier to get into, than out of, these vehicles

parts.words: It may be easier to get into, than out of, these vehicles
parts.note: describes awkward carriages, but the word also means snares, which catch you easily and hold you fast

explanation.surface: A grumble about cramped carriages that are hard to climb down from.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means light two-wheeled carriages pulled by a pony, and also devices for catching animals, which are easy to enter and hard to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Pony carts of this name and snares share the spelling; the snares are what one cannot escape.

clue.text: They give cause for complaint

parts.note: sounds like grievances, but 'complaint' here is an illness, and a doctor's findings name its cause

explanation.surface: A grumble about things that annoy people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' means a grievance on the surface, but here it is an ailment, and the doctor's verdict identifies what causes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A physician's findings identify the disease behind a patient's symptoms.

clue.text: Note about a parent detailed to be a lawgiver

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word is placed around another

parts.note: taken as the word note

indicators.note: read as de-tailed, with its tail (last letter) cut off

parts.note: a mother is a parent

explanation.surface: A memo concerning a parent assigned to make laws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like 'assigned' but reads as de-tailed, docking the parent's last letter; 'about' wraps the note round what remains. The word is a rare Greek term.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece this was a person appointed to frame laws.

clue.text: Not going round in the right direction-on the contrary

definitions.text: Not going round in the right direction-on the contrary

parts.words: Not going round in the right direction-on the contrary
parts.note: sounds like something going the wrong way, but describes a spiral turning to the left rather than the right

explanation.surface: A complaint that something spins the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' means correct on the surface, but means the right-hand side: the answer describes shells that coil leftward.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means left-handed, and of shells, spiralling to the left rather than the usual right.

clue.text: Heraldic advice to a sluggard

definitions.meaning: in heraldry, describing a beast looking backwards over its shoulder
Proverbs says 'Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways', so the advice is to look at, or regard, the ant

explanation.surface: A coat of arms somehow carries a message for a lazy person.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the word as REGARD ANT, echoing the Bible's 'Go to the ant, thou sluggard'.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry a creature shown gazing back over its shoulder is so described; split, the letters tell an idler to study the industrious ant.

clue.text: "They know the worthy-as 'that most immoral man (Kipling)

definitions.text: "They know the worthy-as 'that most immoral man (Kipling)

parts.words: They know the worthy-as 'that most immoral man (Kipling)
parts.note: a line from Kipling's verse with a blank where a military rank stands before 'as'

explanation.surface: A line of Kipling verse with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash for the gap. Kipling's line is 'They know the worthy General as "that most immoral man"', from his Departmental Ditties.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the army's senior officer rank, which fills the quoted Kipling line.

clue.text: "The glow-worm shows the to be near" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "The glow-worm shows the to be near" (Hamlet)

parts.words: The glow-worm shows the to be near" (Hamlet)
parts.note: the Ghost's line in Hamlet before vanishing, with a blank where the word for morning should stand

explanation.surface: A line from Hamlet with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash for the gap. The Ghost says 'The glow-worm shows the matin to be near', the dawn when spirits must leave.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is an old poetic term for morning, related to the dawn church service of the same name.

clue.text: Where the man-servant rises about 6

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, so the words are written backwards

parts.note: a valet is a gentleman's manservant
VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A butler gets up at about six o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rises' turns both VALET and VI upwards, giving TELAV and IV. 'About 6' looks like a time of day but just supplies VI.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue asks for a place, and this Israeli coastal city is one.

clue.text: A terrible way to finish a race

definitions.text: A terrible way to finish a race

parts.words: A terrible way to finish a race
parts.note: suggests a disastrous end to a running event, but 'race' means a people, wiped out entirely

explanation.surface: A runner's dreadful ending to a sprint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' looks like a contest, but it is an ethnic group; 'finish' means destroy.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the deliberate killing of a whole people or nation.

clue.text: " She will start from her slumber When shake the door." (Arnold)

definitions.text: " She will start from her slumber When shake the door." (Arnold)

parts.words: She will start from her slumber When shake the door." (Arnold)
parts.note: a line from Matthew Arnold's poem The Forsaken Merman, with a blank where the wind-blasts should stand

explanation.surface: A line of Matthew Arnold's verse with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash for the gap. Arnold's line is 'When gusts shake the door', from The Forsaken Merman.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means sudden blasts of wind rattling the door in Arnold's poem.

clue.text: Capricious ? Not half!

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Capricious ? Not half! (5)': the island CAPRI is the first half of 'Capricious', but no clue word defines it, so 'Capricious' would be both the fodder and the definition.

clue.text: Used by men of high standing

definitions.text: Used by men of high standing

parts.words: Used by men of high standing
parts.note: 'high standing' suggests social rank, but literally means standing well above the ground on poles

explanation.surface: A remark about what important people make use of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High standing' suggests status, but the men literally stand high, on poles strapped to their legs.
explanation.definitionFit: These are long poles with footrests that lift a walker well above the ground.

clue.text: Isn't it slightly incongruous in The Pickwick Papers ?

indicators.note: in means the letters lie inside the words that follow, running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A reader wonders whether a grand label suits Dickens's comic novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals that the letters lie across 'thE PICkwick'. The clue jokes that a grand heroic label fits a comic book oddly.
explanation.definitionFit: A long heroic narrative is an odd label for Dickens's rambling comic novel, which is the incongruity the clue points at.

clue.text: Hill 60'? So much rubbish!

parts.note: Hill 60 was a mound near Ypres fought over in the First World War, so it was a hill (heap) where a fight (scrap) took place

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at an account of a famous wartime battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Hill 60 near Ypres was a man-made mound bitterly fought over in 1915. Read as 'scrap' (fight) plus 'heap' (hill), the word also means a pile of junk.
explanation.definitionFit: A pile of discarded junk is where useless things end up, and also, split, a hill where fighting happened.

clue.text: He'll be a slippery customer when he grows up

definitions.text: He'll be a slippery customer when he grows up

parts.words: He'll be a slippery customer when he grows up
parts.note: sounds like a forecast about a sly child, but describes a young fish that becomes a literally slimy adult

explanation.surface: A prediction that a crafty boy will become a shifty man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slippery customer' means a devious person, but here it is a slimy eel; the answer is a young eel.
explanation.definitionFit: A juvenile eel grows into the slimy adult fish proverbially hard to hold.

clue.text: The old one is proverbially immortal

definitions.text: The old one is proverbially immortal

parts.words: The old one is proverbially immortal
parts.note: refers to the saying 'old ... never die, they simply fade away'

explanation.surface: A remark about an elderly person who seems to go on forever.
explanation.walkthrough: The song and saying is 'Old soldiers never die'.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying holds that veterans of the army never die but merely fade away.

clue.text: Herb that is dear abroad at six pounds

parts.note: cher is French for dear
VI is six in Roman numerals
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: An expensive herb bought overseas costs six pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' signals a foreign word: French cher.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a parsley-like culinary plant with a mild aniseed flavour.
